content:
EP 266 · 20 MIN LISTEN · 3 MIN READ

Every so often, I’ve been picking something I already sell, giving myself three days, and just selling it.
No new product.
No six-week runway.
No giant launch plan.

Lately I’ve been experimenting with these tiny promotional windows, and it’s changed the way I think about revenue in my business.

It’s also made me realise something most of us are getting wrong.

We don’t need more things to sell.
We need more reasons to sell the things we’ve already made – and with Black Friday coming up, that’s exactly what I want to talk about today.

LINKS MENTIONED

→ Join Black Friday Case Files — free, kicks off Monday

→ Episode 261: Stop Creating New Offers

→ Email Marketing Skool — my free community

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS EPISODE

✅ Why a launch doesn’t have to mean launching something new

✅ How I’m using simple three-day launches in my own business

✅ Why your audience probably hasn’t seen your offer as much as you think they have

✅ What I’d send during a simple three-day promotional window

✅ Different ways to create urgency without automatically discounting

✅ Why Black Friday is a reason to sell, not necessarily a reason to create

A launch doesn’t have to mean launching something new…

Here’s what I want you to sit with for a second: when most of us decide we want to make more money, our brain goes straight to “what can I create?”

A new workshop. A new mini course. A new bundle. Something.

But a launch and a product are two different things.

A launch can simply mean deciding that for the next three days, you’re going to intentionally sell something you already have. That’s it. The product might be six months old, two years old, evergreen, something you’ve sold a hundred times before. The offer doesn’t need to change. The reason to pay attention – that’s what’s new.

I’m a natural creator.
Give me an idea and a day and I’ll happily disappear and come back with a course, a calculator and a sales page to match. Marketing, for me, takes more intention than creating does – and this shift, separating “what can I make” from “what can I sell”, has been the difference this year.

Your audience hasn’t seen it as much as you think

We launch something, send a handful of emails, mention it on the podcast, maybe post about it – and then a month later we think, “well, I can’t talk about that again, everyone’s already seen it.”

Have they, though?

Someone joined your list yesterday. Someone was on holidays when you launched it. Someone saw the email in their inbox while standing in the supermarket line and told themselves they’d check it out later and never did. Someone didn’t have the problem yet. Someone had the problem and didn’t realise your offer solved it.

We confuse our own boredom with audience saturation.

We’ve stared at our own sales page for 47 hours.
We’ve written the emails, built the checkout, taught the course.
To us it feels old. To someone who just found you, it’s brand new.

That gap is where most of the revenue we’re leaving on the table is actually sitting.

What do I actually send during a three-day promotional window?

The constraint is the point. When I know I’ve only got Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, I don’t have time to overcomplicate it – no seventeen-email sequence, no ninety-minute webinar, no five-day challenge.

Just the offer, communicated clearly.

Here’s the shape of it:

Day one – why this, why now.

Name the problem. Explain why it matters. Introduce the offer.

Day two – help me believe.

A customer story, your own story, an objection answered, a behind-the-scenes look at what’s actually inside.

Day three – make the decision.

Remind them what’s happening, summarise the offer, remind them of the deadline, and give them the chance to buy – plus one extra reminder email later that day. Reminding someone something is closing tonight isn’t a crime.

Then it’s done.

I go back to normal emails. Whatever I added for the promotion – a bonus, a lower price – gets taken away again. If you said there were 20 spots, there need to actually be 20 spots. That’s not a nice-to-have, that’s the whole game. It’s how people learn to trust what you say.

Urgency doesn’t have to mean a discount!

When I say give people a reason to buy, I don’t mean slap 70% off on everything. A reason can be the price, but it can just as easily be a bonus, a live Q&A that isn’t normally included, a bundle of two things you already have, a seasonal angle that makes the exact same product suddenly relevant, or simply an upcoming price increase.

Think about your favourite retailer.
They don’t build a new product line every time they want revenue – they already have the products.

What changes is the reason you’re being invited to buy today.
That’s all a promotion is asking your audience to do.

Why Black Friday is a reason to sell, not a reason to create

This is the mistake I see most often heading into Black Friday: “I need to create a Black Friday offer.” Maybe. But before you do, ask what you already have. What’s sitting quietly in your Google Drive right now that could get a Black Friday moment? Could you add a bonus, bundle it, temporarily change the price, or offer access to you?

Black Friday isn’t an excuse to create more – it’s a reason to sell what you’ve already made. Your audience is already expecting offers. There’s already a natural deadline built into the calendar. You don’t have to invent anything except the reason to pay attention.

So before you spend this weekend building something new, go and look at what you’ve already got.
Ask which of it still solves a real problem, and ask yourself honestly when you last actually sold it.
Not linked it in the footer. Not mentioned it in passing.
Actually sold it.

If the answer is months ago, that’s your opportunity.

You might not need another product.
You might just need to give something you’ve already created a red carpet moment.

[00:00:00] Every so often, I’ve been picking something I already sell, giving myself three days, and just selling it. No new product, no six-week runway, no giant launch plan, not creating 17 new bonuses because apparently the thing wasn’t complicated enough already. Just an offer I already know is good, a reason to talk about it again, and a few days where I intentionally put it in front of my audience. And it’s made me realise something.

I don’t think most of us need more things to sell. I think we need more reasons to sell the things that we’ve already made. And with Black Friday coming up soon, I really want to talk about this. Let’s get into it.

Are you a female business owner frustrated with battling the algorithm and looking for growth strategies that don’t involve awkwardly pointing or dancing online or throwing cash at paid ads? Welcome to the Email Growth Show. I’m your host, Kylie Kelly, visibility and email marketing strategist. I grew my email list from zero to almost 10,000 subscribers in less than two years, and the same is possible for you too.

Are you ready to build your email list and start making more money in your online business? Let’s head into today’s episode.

Hey, hey, welcome back to the Email Growth Show. Now, yes, I am still sick. This is the second week of having influenza A. I love that for me. So again, I apologise that you have to listen to me sounding so nasally, but I am so glad that you are here. So if you’ve been listening for a while, you might remember a few episodes ago, I basically told you to stop creating new offers.

If you want to go back and listen to it, it’s episode 261, back on the 7th of August.

[00:02:00] Now, telling you to do this was probably slightly hypocritical coming from me because I do love creating new things. Give me Claude, Canva, a coffee, and an idea, and I will happily disappear for an entire day and emerge with a new course, a calculator, an interactive tool, a sales page, and probably an event to go with it.

I’m actually creating a new website with Claude as we speak. I love creating. But I’ve been really intentionally changing the way I think about my offers this year. Instead of constantly asking, “What can I create next?” I’ve been asking, “What do I already have that I could sell again? What could I improve? What could I update? What could I reposition? What could I put back in front of my audience?” And lately, I’ve been experimenting with these really small promotional windows. Three days. Pick an offer, create a reason, talk about it, close the promotion, and move on. And honestly, it’s been really fun.

I’m really, really enjoying it, not only because they create these lovely little cash injections into the business, right? But also because they’re forcing me to become better at something I think a lot of us avoid: repetition. [00:03:00] We’re so quick to assume people have already seen it. This is something that I see all the time that I used to do myself. We launch something, we send out four or five emails, we’ll mention it on the podcast, we might post about it.

Then a month later we’re thinking, “Well, I can’t talk about that again. Everyone already knows about it.” But do they? Do they really? Because I can almost guarantee they don’t. Somebody joined your email list yesterday. Well, hopefully, if you’re in my world. Somebody was on holidays when you launched it.

Somebody might have seen your email while they were standing in the supermarket line and thought, “Oh, I’ll check this out later.” Someone wasn’t ready for it three months ago. Someone didn’t have the problem yet. Someone had the problem but didn’t realise your offer solved it.

Someone saw the name of the product and never opened the email. And then there are probably hundreds of people who genuinely never saw it at all. But we have seen it. We’ve stared at the sales page for 47 hours. We’ve written the emails. We’ve created the graphics. We’ve built the checkout. We’ve taught the course. [00:04:00] We’ve answered the questions about it. To us, it feels old and done. But to our audience, it might be brand sparkly new. And this is where we make a really expensive mistake. We confuse our own boredom with audience saturation. Let that sink in.

And often we think revenue requires something new. This is the bigger belief underneath it all. When we want to make more money, our brain immediately goes, “Okay, what can I launch?” And by launch, we often mean, what can I create to launch? A new workshop, a new mini course, a new template, a new membership, a new service, a new bundle, a new something.

But what if we separated those two things? Because a launch doesn’t have to mean launching something new. A launch can simply mean, for the next three days, in my case, I’m going to intentionally sell this thing. That’s it. The product can be six months old, it can be two years old, it can be evergreen, it can be something you’ve sold 100 times before.

The offer doesn’t have to be brand new. The reason to pay attention, that can be new. [00:05:00] That’s the shift. That’s the wrapping paper of the whole thing. So let me tell you what I’ve been experimenting with, and it might inspire you. So instead of having a product sitting quietly in my shop hoping somebody happens to stumble across it, I’m giving it moments.

I’m saying, “Okay, this week, this is what I’m talking about,” and I’ll give myself a really short window. So for me, it’s been three days. Enough time for me to tell the story, explain the problem, show people what I’ve created, answer objections, remind them, give them a reason to make a decision, and then we’re done.

I’m not spending six weeks warming people up. I’m not doing a 90-minute webinar. I’m not creating a five-day challenge. I’m not building an elaborate funnel, and importantly, I’m not creating a new product. I’m taking something that already exists and just putting my marketer hat on, and that distinction has been really important for me because I am a natural creator. Marketing, for me, requires more intention.

And this brings me to evergreen offers, right? [00:06:00] Because I think evergreen is sometimes sold to us as: build the funnel, turn it on, disappear, sales will magically happen forever. Lovely. I would love to have one of those, please. Look, evergreen systems absolutely can make sales without you actively launching.

That’s one of the reasons I’m moving more of my business in that direction, in the digital product, high volume, low ticket space. I love that someone can discover me today, join my email list, find an offer, and buy it without waiting for me to launch. But here’s what I think we forget.

Evergreen means someone can buy at any time. It doesn’t mean they’re going to think about buying it at any time. There’s a difference there, because people still need attention. They still need reminders. They still need a reason to act. They still need a bit of urgency to it. Your evergreen offer still needs marketing, and sometimes the easiest way to do that is to take that evergreen product and give it a little moment in the spotlight.

Roll that red carpet out for it for a couple of days, shine a light on it so your audience remembers that it’s there.

[00:07:00] If we think about our favourite retailer — think about a physical shop — they don’t create an entirely new product line every time they want revenue. They already have products. What changes? The reason you’re being invited to buy. There might be an end of season sale, a birthday sale, Mother’s Day, Christmas, Black Friday, New Year, back to school, free shipping weekend, an anniversary, whatever it might be.

The product might be exactly the same product that was sitting there last Tuesday, but now there’s a reason to pay attention to it today. And I think online business owners can learn a lot from that, because we spend so much time making new products and not nearly enough time creating opportunities for people to buy them.

And I do want to add here that the reason doesn’t always have to be a discount. This is especially important with Black Friday incoming soon. So when I say give people a reason to buy, I don’t necessarily mean slash the price, discount everything, stick 70% off in giant red letters.

A reason can be the price, absolutely, but it could also be a bonus. [00:08:00] It could be a live component. Maybe your evergreen course doesn’t usually include access to you, but anyone who joins this weekend gets a live Q&A. It could be a bundle of things. Maybe you package two existing things together. It can be a seasonal angle — the exact same product suddenly becomes incredibly relevant because of what’s happening in your customer’s life right now. It could be an upcoming price increase. It could be access to something that’s normally unavailable. It could be a deadline. It could simply be, “I’m talking about this right now because I think you need it.”

The offer doesn’t need to change. It gets to be simple, but we need to give them a reason. Now, what I have found interesting is this three-day window that I’ve been testing and experimenting with — it’s actually doing something for me too. I didn’t expect this. The short deadline isn’t only useful for the buyer. It’s been really useful for me, because when I know Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and that’s it, I’m far less likely to overcomplicate it. I don’t need a 17 email sequence. I don’t need three months of launch content. I don’t need to completely redesign the product or have some complicated affiliate strategy.

[00:09:00] I don’t have time to make it enormous. So instead I ask, “Okay, what’s the offer? Who is it for? Why do they need it? And why now? What do they need to hear to make a decision?” And then I communicate that. That’s marketing. And I actually think constraints can make us much better marketers, because we don’t have time to hide behind creating more stuff.

So I want to share with you, as we start to wrap this up, what I actually send in a simple three-day launch, because I think this might be helpful. Especially if you’re listening thinking, “Okay Kylie, but what do these three days actually look like?” Again, it gets to be incredibly simple.

Day one is why this, why now. Talk about the problem. Why does it matter? Why are you bringing this particular offer forward right now? What will change for the person if they solve it? Introduce the offer. And I will add, all of this is done just with emails. Normally two emails a day on days one and two, sometimes a third email on day three.

That is it. So day two, [00:10:00] help me believe. This can be proof, a customer story, your own story, an objection, an FAQ, a behind-the-scenes look at what’s actually inside. This is the day where I address what might be stopping somebody who wants this from saying yes. So that’s day two. And then day three is make the decision.

Remind them what’s happening, summarise the offer, remind them of the deadline, and give them the opportunity to buy. Now, I will say, I will send an extra email on the last day. People need reminders. You are not committing an email marketing crime by reminding somebody that something they were interested in is closing tonight. So don’t be afraid to send a few extra emails. Then after those three days, we’re done. I go back to normal emails. I take the bonus or whatever I added, I take it away. I increase the price back to what it was if I discounted it.

Whatever I’ve done for the reason, that’s gone now. And I want to be really clear here, because it’s really important to me that you all know that you need to have integrity with this. If you say there’s 20 spots, [00:11:00] there better be fucking 20 spots. Don’t get caught in a lie just because you’re excited by adding extra to what you say. If it’s limited spots, stick to it. Stick to your word. This means more right now than anything else you can possibly do, because this is how people will start to trust you. They’ll start to know you’re a person of integrity. They’ll start to believe what you send them and what you say. So make sure whatever you say, you stick to it.

So after the three days, we remove the things, or we increase the price back up, or whatever needs to happen, we go back to business as usual. So that’s a launch — three days. It doesn’t have to consume your life and it doesn’t have to make $50,000 either. So this is another thing I really want to normalise. Not every promotion needs to be some giant five-figure launch. Sometimes it might just be a little cash injection into my business. It might be 500 bucks, it might be $1,000, maybe it’s 3,000, maybe it’s more. But if I can create those revenue spikes throughout the year using products that already exist, that starts to add up over time.

Let’s say you did a small promotion and made $1,500. [00:12:00] Then six weeks later, another one makes 2K. Then another one makes 800. Then another one makes 3K. Those aren’t necessarily sexy “I made $100,000 in 24 hours” screenshots. But A, they’re probably bullshit, and B, we’re building real businesses here, and those smaller revenue moments compound too.

They matter just as much as the big ones. This is something I’ve been thinking about a lot this year. As you know, I’m moving from high ticket into a high volume, low ticket space, so my income has shifted dramatically and it’s been a real work in progress to regulate my nervous system through it, and also to recognise that actually, let’s celebrate the small wins as much as we celebrate the big ones.

Let’s celebrate the 50 bucks that comes in as much as we celebrate the big stuff. The other thing that excites me about this — if you’re getting a lot of these smaller payments in, it means you’re getting more people. More people trusting you, more people purchasing, more buyers in your ecosystem.

That is never a bad thing. I would rather have an ecosystem full of 100 buyers that bought a $50 product than, like, two high ticket buyers in my whole list. [00:13:00] It’s setting me up for the future, and it can do the same for you as well. So let’s start to look at any money that comes into your business with a grateful heart and actually recognise how powerful it is when money can easily come in, when ideal clients can easily come in.

I also think it’s important to diversify the way that money can enter the business. We want evergreen sales, small promotions, a bit of affiliate income, a community, products, occasional bigger launches, different revenue moments. This is going to make your nervous system feel so safe, because we’re not putting all our eggs into one basket.

It’s going to feel so much safer for you, and honestly, a lot more fun as well.

Now, another reason I love selling existing offers repeatedly is because every time you promote something, you learn. You learn which subject line got opened, which story got replies, which objections keep coming up, which bonuses people care about, which part of the sales page confused them.

You learn what language they use, what angles made somebody suddenly say, “Oh my gosh, that’s exactly what I need.” If you launch an offer once and then abandon it because it didn’t immediately become your million-dollar signature program, you throw away all of that information. [00:14:00] But if you sell it again, now you can improve it.

Sell it again, improve it. Sell it again, improve it. This is how offers get good. Not because you magically nailed everything in version one, but because you gave the thing enough chances to teach you how to sell it to your ideal clients. Now, this brings me to Black Friday, and obviously there’s a reason I’m talking about this right now.

We are heading towards Black Friday. At the time of recording this, we are 78 days away. And I think one of the biggest mistakes people make with Black Friday is thinking, “I need to create a Black Friday offer.” Do you? You might. If you’ve got an amazing idea and strategically it makes sense, sure, go for it. But most people listening to this, I would start with, “What do I already have? What solves a problem?

What have people bought before? What do customers love? What’s sitting quietly in my Google Drive right now? Could I give that a Black Friday moment? Could I add a bonus or bundle it with something else, or temporarily change the price, or create a fast action version, or give people access to me as a bonus?

Could I simply put it back in front of my audience with a really [00:15:00] compelling reason to buy?” That is so much simpler than spending the next two months frantically creating something new from scratch. And this is really the whole point of today’s episode. Black Friday is a reason. Black Friday isn’t necessarily an excuse to create more, it’s a reason to sell.

No matter who you serve, your audience is already expecting offers. People are already in buying mode. There’s already a natural deadline. There’s already an event happening in the marketplace that you get to participate in. The reason is built in. You don’t have to invent anything. And I know that is such an opportunity for small business owners — not to become Amazon, not to discount your entire business into oblivion, but to intentionally say, “Here is something I already know can help you, and here’s why now is a really good time to get it.”

That is it. Which brings me to what’s happening on Monday. The Black Friday Case Files kicks off. These are short, focused conversations where we’re looking at real Black Friday promotions — what they sold, what they [00:16:00] did, what worked, what didn’t, what they’d change, and what they would do again. Because I think seeing real examples makes this so much easier. You can look at someone else’s promotion and think, “Oh, I could do that,” or “that’s way too complicated for me,” or “I love that part, but I might change this.” And that’s what I wanted. I don’t want you copying somebody else’s Black Friday campaign, but I want you to see what’s possible and then build something that makes sense for your business.

So I’ll put the link to join in the show notes of this episode. It’s free all of next week. Go and check it out, and we kick off on Monday. And then I do have something else coming too. So if you listen to the Case Files and think, “Okay Kylie, I’m convinced I want to do something for Black Friday, but can somebody please just tell me what to do?”

I’ve got you, because after the Case Files finishes, I’ll be opening up Black Friday Made Simple, and the cue is very much in the name. This is not Black Friday made into a 97-step funnel that consumes your entire November. No, no, thank you. This is about helping you choose the offer, create the promotion, plan the emails, and get the thing out into the world without turning [00:17:00] Black Friday into a full-time job.

I’ll tell you more about that very soon, but right now, the first step: come and join Black Friday Case Files next week, and then keep an eye on your emails for Black Friday Made Simple after that. Now, before you go, whether you’re doing Black Friday this year or not, I want you to do something after you finish this episode.

Open wherever you keep your offers — your website, Teachery, ThriveCart, a spreadsheet, whatever. Look at what you’ve already got, not through the eyes of the creator who’s bored with it all. I know what that looks like. I want you to look through the eyes of somebody who just discovered you yesterday. Ask yourself, “Which of these things still solves a real problem?”

Then ask yourself, “When was the last time I actually sold it?” Not just linked it in the footer, not mentioned it in passing, not hoped somebody would stumble across the sales page — actually sold the thing. If the answer is, um, six months ago, that’s your opportunity. You might not need another product. [00:18:00] You might not need another course or lead magnet. You might just need to give something you already created a red carpet moment. And that’s the thought I want to leave you with today.

Remember, a launch doesn’t have to mean launching something new. Sometimes a launch is simply deciding, for the next three days, I’m going to stop hiding this thing and I’m going to tell people why I made it, who it’s for, how it can help, and I’m going to give them a reason to make a decision.

Then I’m going to move on. And if Black Friday can be that reason for you this year, amazing. Come and join Black Friday Case Files starting Monday. Again, everything you need is in the show notes. But please, do not spend this weekend creating another offer. Go and look at what you’ve already got.

You might be sitting on the exact thing you need to sell next. All right, my loves. That is all for this episode. I hope you found it helpful, and as always, I will see you next week. Hopefully you’ll be listening to a healthy-sounding Kylie. All right, bye for now.

[00:19:00] Thank you so much for tuning into this episode of the Email Growth Show. I hope you found valuable insights into the next steps you can take to grow your email list and boost your business without relying on social media or paid ads. If you enjoyed this episode, please take a moment to rate and review the show and share it with others.

Your feedback helps me reach more female entrepreneurs just like you who are ready to say goodbye to social media and leverage email marketing to grow their business and make a bigger impact. Thank you so much for listening, and I’ll see you in the next episode.

content:
EP 265 · 26 MIN LISTEN · 4 MIN READ

Back in 2022, when I was barely getting this business off the ground, I ran these tiny audio pop-up events that grew my email list by 100 to 150 people at a time.

I decided to bring them back this year – small, low-lift, one a month.

The first one is done and dusted, and I’ve got the real numbers, including the part that didn’t work quite as well as I’d hoped.

So today: what actually happened when I ran my first Behind the Biz pop-up, why I chose scrappy audio over another big summit, and where I actually find the people I collaborate with (hint: it’s not magic)

LINKS MENTIONED

→ Join the Black Friday Case Files waitlist (live Sept 14 – 18): https://listen.kyliekelly.com

→ Digital Shop: https://shop.kyliekelly.com

→ Free Resource: Your Next 1000 Subscribers Instant Access Here

→ My Free Community: Email Marketing Skool

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS EPISODE

✅ Why I chose scrappy Voxer-style audio interviews over a big polished summit

✅ The real August numbers – 303 signups, 370+ downloads, and just one $97 season pass sale

✅ Why a “failed” launch metric doesn’t mean the event failed

✅ How much the event actually warmed people up for my Break Up With Instagram launch

✅ Exactly how I find new collaborators without cold-pitching strangers

Why I brought back low-lift audio pop-ups (instead of another big summit)

I could have made this a full summit. Video interviews, speaker pages, everyone recording a 30-minute presentation – I’ve done that before, and there’s nothing wrong with it. But I’m in a season of asking myself how I can get the result without making the thing enormous…

So I went back to something I already knew worked: Voxer-style interviews.

I send a voice note question, the guest answers when they have time, I reply when I have time, and it goes back and forth asynchronously. No calendar tetris between Australia and the US, no 5am Zoom calls. I download the audio, clean it up a little, and that’s basically the whole production process.

I also like that it doesn’t sound perfectly polished.
There are pauses, background noise, someone stumbling over a word. It sounds like two business friends sending voice notes back and forth, and you happen to have access to the conversation. When the topic is something like real Black Friday numbers, I want it to feel exactly like that – not a conference stage.

The real numbers from my event (the good and the humbling)

The August audience growth event wrapped up last week, and here’s what actually happened.

303 people signed up for the free event, with eight speakers, each sending just one email. The podcast feed picked up 370+ downloads – not counting the people who listened straight from the webpage.

Then there’s the season pass – lifetime access to all five events for $97. I announced it on opening night to roughly 100 people. I sold one. Just one. (Thank you, Colie.)

I could have left that number out and just told you about the 303 signups. But if we’re actually talking business, the useful question is whether it made money – and mostly, it didn’t. That doesn’t mean the event failed. That was never the job it had in the first place!

What a “free” event was actually for…

I built these pop-ups to do three things: nurture my list with something fun and different, test a repeatable event format that doesn’t wipe me out, and warm people up for my Break Up With Instagram mini-course launch.

On the first two, it delivered.
On the third, about 30% of the people who bought the mini-course had listened to the event first – real overlap, but I’d have liked it higher.

That tells me something useful: either the bridge between the event and the offer wasn’t strong enough, or an event about audience growth in general was too broad a lead-in for an Instagram-specific offer. Both good things to know before I build the next one.

How I actually find new collaborators

The question I get most since hosting this event is where I find people to collaborate with. The truth is I deliberately avoid working with the same 15 people over and over – otherwise every event just circulates the same audience back through itself.

My biggest source is watching who else shows up in a bundle or summit I’m already part of – they’ve already said yes to promotion and borrowed audiences, so it’s a warm pool. I’ll follow them, read their emails, watch how they treat people, sometimes for six months before I ever pitch them anything.

I also scroll with intention – looking for smart replies and different perspectives instead of doom-scrolling – and occasionally drop a callout in a collaboration Facebook group when I need a couple of fresh voices, which is exactly how I found two new guests for the next event.

Remember your network keeps compounding… every summit, bundle or podcast guest spot puts you next to another group of business owners you didn’t have access to before. You won’t always be able to measure the value of a relationship in the week it starts – sometimes the real payoff shows up six months later.

Building a growth engine, not chasing one big win

One event isn’t the story here – five of them, run back to back through the rest of the year, is. 303 people here, a podcast interview that brings 40 there, another event that brings 200 – that’s how a list actually compounds, without needing one single thing to be “the thing.”

It was successful, but there were parts that worked really well, parts that didn’t quite do as I’d hoped they would, and quite a few things that I’m changing or paying attention to as I do the next one.

So today I thought I would pull back the curtain on the August Behind the Biz sessions. This was my [00:02:00] August pop-up audio event, and I’m doing these events monthly around a specific topic. August was all about audience growth. The one that is in two weeks’ time in September is called the Black Friday Case Files, and then I’ve got more planned for October, November, and December.

Because I know sometimes when you see someone hosting events or doing bundles or bringing podcast guests in, it can look like they just magically know hundreds of people. To be clear, I do not magically know hundreds of people. There is a strategy behind it, so we’re gonna talk about that too.

So before we talk about the event itself, I’m gonna talk about why I chose audio. Because technically I could have done this as a summit, right? [00:03:00] I could have had video interviews. I could have hosted live sessions. I could have made beautiful speaker pages that had everyone record 30-minute presentations and gone the whole nine yards.

I am in a season where I’m asking myself a lot, like, how can I get the result without making this thing enormous? Like, how can I make something good without it requiring so many moving pieces? We also have some personal things that are going on at the moment. And so again, in this season of life — with whatever that looks like for me, for you — like how can we make this feel light? Yes, there’s always work involved, but how can we do it in a way that feels really good for us?

How can I grow my audience without creating another job for myself, right? You know, I love a project. You guys know that about me. Give me half a reason and I’ll invent a whole event by lunchtime, right? And sometimes [00:04:00] that is brilliant. Sometimes my multi-passionate heart just loves nothing more than that.

Sometimes though, that’s also how you can end up exhausted because you’ve accidentally created a three-week launch and 19 bases when all I actually needed was a simple collaboration. So with these pop-ups, one of my rules was that they needed to stay small, low lift, easy for me, easy for the speaker, easy for the person listening.

So that brought me back to something that I’ve actually done before, which is Voxer-style interviews. Because I’m in Australia, most of the people I collaborate with are not. I’ve got connections in the US, Canada, Europe, the UK, like all over the place, and anybody who’s tried to schedule a Zoom interview between Australia and the US or the UK knows it can very quickly end with somebody needing to get up at 5:00 AM, and no thank you, I have never been a part of the 5:00 AM club, and [00:05:00] Zoom is not gonna make me start.

So Voxer completely removes that. I literally send them a voice note question, they answer when they have time, I reply when I have time, and it goes back and forward asynchronously, right? Then at the end, I download the audio, I clean it up a little, and that’s basically it. There’s no calendar tetris, there’s no Zoom rooms, there’s no like, “Oh my gosh, now my kid is sick and I can’t make it.” Like, “I’m sick, I can’t make it.” There’s none of that. And I want to add, from the speaker’s point of view, it’s a really easy yes as well. And that matters to me too, because when we talk about collaborations, we often think about what’s in it for us. How many subscribers can I get? How much exposure will I get? Will they be promoting me? [00:06:00] And of course, that is the motivation behind creating these audience growth events. Of course it is. But I think the easier that you can make a collaboration for the other person, the easier it becomes to get really good people involved.

And with these interviews, I’m not asking someone to create a presentation. I’m not asking them to make slides or rehearse a workshop. And I think another reason why I love this Voxer format — which is a bit harder to explain until you listen to it — but the audio’s not perfect, and I actually like that. It sounds like Voxer. It does not sound like two people sitting in a podcast studio, and I used to think that was something I had to fix. Like, maybe I needed to make it cleaner or more polished. And when the topic is something like audience growth, or particularly this next one, all about Black Friday, where I’m asking people to share real numbers and talk about something that worked or something that completely flopped, I actually want it to feel like that. I don’t want it to feel like a conference presentation, right? Because people say different things when they feel like they’re having a conversation. You get the bit where they go like, “Oh my God, can I tell you what really happened?” Oh, that’s the good stuff. That’s the stuff I want. I want the real life.

And so I clean up the recordings a little bit, yes. But I do leave a lot of that natural texture in there because I think it’s what makes the whole thing way more human, which I love.

Okay, let’s talk about what happened in the August event. So it literally just wrapped up last week, and I’m really excited to share with you the numbers. So just like normal, I wanna give you the real numbers, the real story, what really happened, because again, it is not just the highlight reel over here.

So the audience growth event ran last week. I had 303 people sign up for the free event, which [00:08:00] I was really happy with. You gotta keep in mind that we had eight speakers, so it was really small, really quite intimate — it’s not this massive summit campaign, right? Like, I wasn’t running around for six weeks promoting it. It was literally eight of us, and they all sent one email, and that was kind of it.

So 303 people saying, “Yes, I want access to this little audio series,” fantastic. The podcast feed itself got over 370 downloads, and that doesn’t include people who listened directly through the webpage I created, so the actual listens would’ve been higher than that. Again, really happy with that. That tells me the consumption was there. They weren’t just signing up and then not getting to it. They were signing up with the intention of, “Oh, let me tune into this,” which I think is really great. I never want to host something where people just sign up and disappear. I want them to consume it because it’s really valuable information. I never put out anything that’s not, right? Like, there’s no point. We don’t have enough time. I’m not gonna waste yours by putting out something without any meat in it. I always put out something that I would [00:09:00] find really valuable in one part of my journey or another.

If you think about it in terms of numbers — if you have an event where 2,000 people register but only 47 people listen, I’m not sure we’ve actually built much of anything. Whereas when a good percentage of the people who opt in actually spend time with your content, now we’ve got something. They’re hearing my voice. They’re hearing the voices of the speakers. They’re learning something. They’re becoming more familiar with my world. That’s relationship building. That’s what we’re aiming for.

Then we have the season pass. Now, this is where the story gets much less impressive. So the season pass was an idea I had, a little bit late, mind you, but I had a few people asking, “Oh, how can I get ongoing access to this? Do you have anything I can buy to get access after the end of the week?” So I was like, “Oh my gosh, amazing opportunity, I’ll create a season pass. I’m doing these events monthly. The season pass will give them lifetime access to all of the interviews forever, for all of them. All five events, they get access to [00:10:00] all of the things.”

I sold one. One season pass. I announced it on the opening night to roughly 100 people at that point. It was a little bit over 100 people when the event kicked off. More came throughout the week, but it was about 100 people. One person bought it, and I know the person really well. Shout out, Colie. I really appreciate you. But yeah, one person. Ta-da. Massive launch, right? $97.

Now, I’m telling you this because I could have very easily left that number out, right? I could have just said, “We had 303 people register, over 370 downloads. Look at this fabulous event that I hosted that was really easy.” But if we are actually talking about business and marketing, I think the useful question is: did it make money? Technically, yes, I had one sale. But no, the season pass itself did not suddenly become this enormous revenue stream.

Now, that doesn’t actually reflect anything on the event. It doesn’t mean the event failed. And this is something that I really wanted to mention because sometimes we [00:11:00] accidentally judge something against a job it was never designed to do. We make a free event and then go, “Oh, well it didn’t make $10,000, so it was a waste of time.” Was making $10,000 the job that you gave the event? Like, was it a revenue-generating event? Was that the main purpose? Because if it wasn’t, that’s kind of a weird scorecard to keep, right?

As an example, when I created these pop-up audio events, there were three things that I wanted them to do. One was nurture. I wanted a reason to give my list something fun, something different, something useful, something that I was hosting — not another PDF, not another training, but something they could go for a walk and have a quick listen and learn something. Something they could listen to when they were driving or picking up the kids or making dinner, and it did that.

The second thing was that I wanted to test a repeatable event format that didn’t wipe me out. This is actually a bigger goal for me than it might sound. I have hosted a lot of events. I know how to make a big splash, but I am trying to get better at creating things that compound without me needing to [00:12:00] summon launch-level energy every time. Because again, I have pretty ambitious list growth goals, right? I wanna double my email list by the end of the year. And here we are in September and I am nowhere near where I wanna be yet.

So rather than throwing that goal away and saying, “Well, maybe I’ll do it next year,” I’m looking at the remaining months and thinking, “Okay, what levers can I pull? What can I repeat? What can I test? What can I create once and make easier every time I do it?” And these monthly pop-ups are one of those levers. Now, thanks to AI, they’re getting even easier to create a system around and make rinse and repeat, which is so exciting.

So my plan over the next few months, right — I ran one in August. I’m running the Black Friday Case Files in September. The link to join the waitlist is in the show notes. I’m running that in September. I’m running another one in October, then November, and then December. Now, I’m not [00:13:00] judging one event. What I’m actually doing is building a little growth engine, and that is very different.

Often we want one giant answer. We’d love to have one giant launch or a lead magnet that suddenly explodes or a collaboration that brings in 5,000 subscribers at a time or whatnot. And I mean, that would be great, fucking fantastic. I wouldn’t say no. But a lot of growth actually comes from stacking small things. 303 here, 150 there, a podcast interview that brings in 40 people, a freebie swap that brings in 70, another event might bring in 200. And suddenly you’ve added 1,000 people without any one thing needing to become the thing. That is much more how I think about audience growth, right? It’s not one door. It’s lots of doors. We’ve talked about this a lot over the last few weeks.

Now the last reason that I ran this August event was that I had my Instagram mini-course coming up. So I created a mini-course called Break Up With [00:14:00] Instagram. I’m so proud of it, I must say. Every time I create a little course I’m trying to make it better than the last one.

50 A Day, fantastic, absolutely loved it. Break Up With Instagram, oh, it’s just that little bit better. Better tools, just a little bit better step by step. I think every time my teaching gets better.

But I thought the audience growth event could act as a bit of a warm-up for that mini-course launch, which made a lot of sense on paper, right? People are listening to conversations about growing their audience, then I have this offer about breaking up with Instagram. Nice little bridge. And did it work? Kind of. About 30% of people who bought the Break Up With Instagram mini-course had listened to the event. So there was definitely overlap. Did I actually talk about the course enough? [00:15:00] Did people see the relationship between those two things?” Or perhaps Breaking Up With Instagram was too narrow of an offer for an event that was about audience growth more generally, right? So there are the questions that I’m asking now.

So the launch for Break Up With Instagram is just about to end. The people that bought, where they came from, what emails they got, what emails they bought from, the heat maps from the checkout page where people were clicking. I look at everything because more than anything, we just need information. And this is why experiments are so useful, because they don’t need to be perfect, but they give us a lot of information. So I can definitely say the August pop-up did a really nice job of nurturing. It did a pretty decent job of growing the audience. It was genuinely low lift, and it did some warming up for the launch. But if I was thinking about it in [00:16:00] terms of a sales funnel for the course, I definitely wouldn’t call it a win. And I’m okay with that, right? ‘Cause it was never created just to do that.

To learn, and I’m excited ’cause the next event is in two weeks’ time. It’s called the Black Friday Case Files. It’s running from September 14 to 18, and I am ridiculously excited about this one, because the premise is really simple. I’ve invited business owners to come on and talk about one Black Friday promotion — either that worked really well or that went horribly.

And I actually wanted both, right? I didn’t just want, “Oh, I made 80K in four days and everything was perfect.” Cool, I’m really happy for you, amazing story. But I also wanted the ones that were like, “Oh, I tried this and it went horribly wrong. I spent three weeks building it and made two sales.” There’s so much to learn from those stories too. I wanna know, like, what would they do differently? What was the offer? Was it the timing? Was it the audience? Was their list not growing before the offer? Did they make it too complicated? The biggest one is that I’m very conscious about not continually collaborating with the exact same people all of the time. Now, of course, I have people I adore working with, and of course I will collaborate with them again. I’m not saying you need a brand-new group every single time, but if every summit you do has the same 20 people, and every bundle you do has the same contributors, and every freebie swap you do is with the same five friends, eventually you are all talking to the same audience over and over again. You are circulating people around [00:18:00] that same little ecosystem. And if the point is audience growth, that becomes a problem.

So I deliberately look for new circles. One way that I do that is incredibly simple. Whenever I am in a bundle or a summit or a collaborative event as a participant, I pay attention to who else is there, because those people are already collaboration-friendly — they’ve already said yes to being in a bundle or a summit or whatever they’re in, they understand promotion, they understand borrowed audiences, and maybe I haven’t personally worked with them yet.

So I’ll look through the speaker list. Who do I like? Whose topic makes sense? Who has an audience that overlaps with mine without it being exactly the same? Who feels like somebody my audience would enjoy learning from? And sometimes that person goes into my world for six months before I ever invite them to anything. I might subscribe to their emails. I might listen to their podcast. I might reply to something. I might follow them on Threads. I’ll see how they talk to people, because — and this is a really important part for me — I don’t wanna work with somebody simply because they [00:19:00] have an email list. I wanna know, do I actually like how this person runs their business? Do our values line up? Would I feel comfortable introducing them to you? Do they teach in a way I respect? Because when you invite someone into your event or to do something with you, you are lending them some of your trust, and I take that really fucking seriously. That is why I’m probably slower about collaborator outreach than some people.

I’m not usually cold-emailing 100 people with, “Hey, do you wanna join my summit?” I want some relationship built there first. And people often hear like, “Oh, relationship before pitch,” and assume that means it’s just a tactic to get a yes. It really isn’t for me. Of course it helps the pitch. It helps if somebody knows who you are. They’re more likely to open their email and say yes. But I’m also using that relationship period to decide whether I want to pitch them. There are plenty of times when it’s a no for me.

So there’s that. Another place I find people is literally while I’m scrolling. Now, I [00:20:00] know I teach a lot about not relying on social media. That doesn’t mean I think social media has no use. It can be brilliant for discovery for this reason. So sometimes when I’m scrolling on Instagram, or if I’m over on Threads, rather than mindlessly consuming, I’ll be looking for people that are saying something smart, who keeps showing up in replies, who has a bit of a different perspective. Even other friends that I have — who do they keep talking about? I use it for research. You know I’m not creating 47 reels over there, but I’m looking for humans.

And often I’ll do this just on occasion when the kids are watching TV or eating dinner or something, and they want me to sit with them, but I probably don’t wanna be watching SpongeBob SquarePants anymore. So I’ll do some research. And when I find somebody I get a bit curious about, I’ll go and join their email list. If they have a podcast or a website, I’ll go and check them out a little bit, because whilst I might discover them on social, it’s usually not where I want the entire relationship to live. So that’s something else I’ll [00:21:00] do to find new people that are outside of my circle.

And then the other place as well is Facebook groups. So I don’t normally use Facebook groups that often, but occasionally, if I just have a few speaker spots open, I will drop a post in a few collaboration or speaker Facebook groups. So as an example, for the Black Friday Case Files, I had a couple of guest spots open. I wanted some fresh voices. So I posted in a Facebook group and was basically like, “This is what I’m doing. This is what I’m looking for. This is the topic. If you’ve got an interesting Black Friday story, let me know.” And it worked. I found two people who had never been involved in one of my events before, which is exactly what I wanted.

Now I wouldn’t do that for every spot, particularly ’cause I’m keeping these events small and curated. I don’t want 30 speakers, right? Like I want five to eight that I personally would vouch for. So that was really helpful to lean on to fill those last couple of gaps.

Okay, so if you’re listening to this thinking, “Okay, Kylie, that sounds lovely for you because you already know people,” I do wanna push back on that slightly, because yes, [00:22:00] at this stage of my business, I do have a network, but the network exists because I have been building it for years. It did not just appear.

I want you to be thinking that every collaboration that you’re in has the potential to create another relationship, right? Every summit you participate in puts you next to another group of business owners. Every podcast you guest on introduces you to the host. Every time you’re in a bundle, there are 20 other contributors that you could potentially connect with. Your network compounds too, and this is why I get a little twitchy when people approach collaborations purely as, “Ooh, how many subscribers can I get?” Sometimes the subscriber number is not the bigger result or the biggest win.

Sometimes you might join a bundle and get fuck all subscribers. It might not be a good fit for that. But you might meet someone in that bundle who later invites you onto their podcast and then introduces you to somebody else, and six months later, you run an event together and you bring in 400 subscribers, right? You cannot always measure the value of a relationship in the week that it starts. That [00:23:00] is why I love this style of growth, right? It has layers. It gives you the immediate audience growth, but it grows your network, it creates future opportunities, it makes business feel a lot less lonely.

It’s honestly the best way. It’s the best way to grow your business. That’s where I’m at with these Behind the Biz sessions. One event down, 303 registrations, 370-plus downloads, one lonely little season pass sale. Again, thank you, Colie. Some core sales that were definitely warmed up through the event. A format that I now know I can run without wanting to throw my laptop out of the window, and four more months to test it.

And I don’t know what the final verdict on this will be, right? Maybe by the end of the year I’ll be like, “Oh, this was the best thing that I did in my business in 2026.” Who the fuck knows, right? But what I can guarantee is I’m gonna learn a lot. I’m testing so many different things each time, I’m gonna know a lot. I’m gonna have a lot of information and data to look at to make decisions then for 2027, which is really exciting.

So if you are [00:24:00] starting something new right now, I want to encourage you: experiment. Look at the numbers. Keep what works, change what doesn’t, and then try it again. That is what business looks like for me most of the time. It’s not like I discovered this seven-step secret, and now everything works perfectly. It’s never that easy. It’s always like, “Hmm, this part worked, that part didn’t. Let’s try it again. Let’s do another version.” So for me, the next version is the Black Friday Case Files running September 14 to 18.

And then I’m gonna keep sharing these results as we go throughout the year, because I think it’s gonna be really fun to see what happens when we have four or five of these to compare, instead of judging everything from one event.

And maybe there’s something in this episode for you too. Maybe you don’t need to build a giant summit. Maybe your version is three people in a private podcast feed. Maybe it’s four experts answering one question. Maybe it’s a tiny email series. Maybe it’s a collaborative workshop. Maybe the thing you need isn’t bigger. Maybe it just needs [00:25:00] to be repeatable. And maybe instead of asking, “What could I launch?” the better question is, “What could I run again?”

Okay, I will leave you with that.

Thank you for listening to this nasally version of myself. Again, if you want to see the Black Friday Case Files in action, the link to join the waitlist is in the show notes. And if this episode has made you realise that you need some fresh people in your collaboration world, maybe spend 10 minutes today doing something really simple. Look at the people sitting beside you in the bundles, the summits, the communities and events you’re already a part of. Not just the host — the other contributors. There are probably some really good relationships sitting right there that you haven’t started yet. Send a message, make a connection, and just trust that it will all grow from there.

All right, my loves, I love you so much. I hope you found this interesting, and I will see you again next week. Bye for now.

[00:26:00] Thank you so much for tuning into this episode of the Email Growth Show. I hope you found valuable insights into the next steps you can take to grow your email list and boost your business without relying on social media or paid ads. If you enjoyed this episode, please take a moment to rate and review the show and share it with others. Your feedback helps me reach more female entrepreneurs just like you, who are ready to say goodbye to social media and leverage email marketing to grow their business and make a bigger impact. Thank you so much for listening, and I’ll see you in the next episode.

✅ The small habits that stop your Claude account running out of tokens

✅ How Anita built a full sales page – copy, design and all – in under two hours

The human-AI sandwich (why you should never just copy-paste AI output)

The idea Anita kept coming back to is what she calls the human-AI sandwich.

You start with the human element – you tell AI what you want, you give it context, you give it your messy thinking.
Then you let AI do a fair chunk of the work.
Then you bring it back and humanise it again before it ever goes out the door.

“AI should never think for us – it should think with us.”

That last step matters more than people think.

You can absolutely train an AI to sound like you – but Anita still goes back through and changes the odd word, adds her own nuance, puts herself back into it.

Never copy and paste AI verbatim. It can draft your copy. It shouldn’t be the last voice in the room.

Claude.ai vs Claude Code vs the Chrome extension – what’s actually different

There are three ways into Claude, and most people only ever meet the first one.

Claude.ai is the regular website or app version, and for most people, that’s genuinely enough.

Claude Code is a different interface entirely – it talks to the files on your computer in real time, which means it can actually build things: sales pages, waitlist pages, calculators, whole apps. You have to give it permission and set the parameters, but once it’s trained, you can hand it real work.

Then there’s the Chrome extension – or in Anita’s case, the Brave browser version. It sits in your sidebar and reads whatever site you’re currently on. She used to open client websites in it and ask it to flag every broken link, every button, every piece of copy that needed work – instant, unpaid research assistant. It’s also just a lighter, faster way in: fewer steps between you and the answer means fewer tokens burned getting there.

Projects: the Claude feature most people skip

Inside Claude.ai, a project is essentially its own island. Anything you upload or discuss inside it stays inside it – nothing leaks out, and nothing from your regular chats leaks in. Anita keeps her business branding in its own project, her email marketing in another, so none of it gets muddied by whatever market research or random thought she’s feeding Claude that day.

The payoff is that you only have to explain who you are once.
Upload a text file or markdown doc with your brand story, your offers, your voice – and every new chat inside that project already knows it. You’re not starting from zero every single time.

The small habits that stop your tokens running out

If you’ve ever wondered why you seem to run out of usage after “only” a few questions, it’s because Claude reads the entire conversation from the start, every single time – including a chat that’s been running for two weeks.

A few things Anita does differently:

  • She avoids feeding it PDFs, which are heavy on tokens – instead she copies the text out and drops that in directly.
  • If she’s working from a Google Doc, she downloads it as a markdown file first, which any AI reads far more efficiently &
  • When a chat gets long, she asks for a handoff summary and starts fresh rather than dragging the whole history along with her.

What this actually looks like in practice…

Anita’s membership sales page is the clearest example.

She trained a copywriting skill on her own voice, gave it a brief, and let it draft the copy – that part took about 45 minutes to review and humanise.
She fed the finished copy back into Claude Code, along with the images to choose from, and told it to build.
Thirty-one minutes later, while she was having dinner, it was done. Padding, spacing, layout – the parts that usually eat entire days for someone who actually does web design – handled in under two hours, start to finish!

She’s also built an income calculator that reverse-engineers how many sales she needs to hit a goal, and a scheduled task that reads her end-of-day voice notes and emails her every Friday afternoon celebrating everything she got done that week.

Small builds, real time back.

But I think there’s a much better question to be asking: not “how do I get a bigger audience”, but “how many ways can the right person discover me”. Those are not the same thing, and today I want to show you why building more doors into your business might be one of the smartest moves you can make right now.

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS EPISODE

✅ The difference between audience size and audience security

✅ The “doors” framework for building a business that doesn’t rely on one platform

✅ How to get more mileage from what you’ve already created, instead of making more

✅ The exact action step: how to audit your doors

Why your offer probably isn’t the problem

You launch something. Three people buy. And the story you tell yourself is instant: “No one wants this.” Maybe your niche is wrong. Maybe you need another certification. Maybe you should scrap it and build something new.

But before you rewrite the offer, ask a different question: how many people actually saw it? If 80 people saw your launch, that’s not evidence nobody wants what you sell. That’s evidence 80 people saw it. Sometimes what looks like an offer problem is really a discovery problem wearing an offer problem’s clothes.

Picture the most beautiful little shop – gorgeous stock, fair prices, a genuinely great experience – hidden down a side street with no sign, no listing on Google Maps, no foot traffic and no website. At the end of the month you’d never say “no one wants my products”. You’d say “no one knows this shop exists”.

Online, we’re incredibly quick to change what’s inside the shop when what we actually need is more traffic finding the door.

Audience size isn’t the same thing as audience security…

Visibility used to feel like a daily task to me: wake up, figure out how to get seen today, post, promote, repeat. Increasingly I think about visibility as infrastructure instead – things you build once that keep creating opportunities for discovery long after you’ve stopped actively working on them.

Audience size isn’t the same thing as audience security.

Someone can have 150,000 followers and feel completely “sorted” – until the platform changes its algorithm and that huge audience stops seeing anything they post. If 90% of your new audience comes from one place, that’s fragile, even while it’s working brilliantly.

Security comes from having more than one way in.

The doors framework

Imagine your business as that same little shop, but instead of one entrance, it has ten doors: podcast, Google, guest recommendations, summits, referrals, Pinterest, PR, a friend’s email forward, Instagram, a collaboration. If one door has a bad month, that’s annoying – but you’re fine, because people are still walking through the other nine.

You don’t need ten doors by Friday. You build one, get it working, then build another. Some doors will bring in loads of the wrong people – close them. Some tiny door you almost didn’t bother building will send you incredible customers again and again – make that one bigger.

This is why tracking where your best people actually come from matters so much over time.

And these doors don’t work in isolation – they compound. Someone hears you on another person’s podcast, searches your name, finds your show, joins your email list, comes to a summit two months later, then eventually buys. Every single one of those touch points played a part. That’s why judging one email or one post by whether it produced an immediate sale misses the point entirely – it’s one step in a much longer path.

You probably don’t need more content – you need more distribution

Creating content has never been easier, which means simply creating something isn’t a strategy anymore. The real question is: who’s going to see it?

You can make the best thing in the world, and if nobody discovers it, it helps no one.

So before you create anything new, look at what you already have. A hundred blog posts. Fifty podcast episodes. A great lead magnet.

The move usually isn’t “what should I make this week” – it’s “how do I build another path to something I’ve already made”. Guest on a podcast and link to an existing resource. Update an old post for SEO. Pin something you already have. Pitch yourself for PR.

You’re not creating more – you’re increasing distribution, and that’s the shift that actually moves the needle right now.

Your next step: audit your doors

Write down every real way someone can discover you today – not what you wish you were doing, what’s actually true.

Google, Pinterest, your podcast, someone else’s podcast, referrals, collaborations, bundles, summits, PR, a newsletter recommendation…

Then be honest about which of those doors are actually open (a blog you haven’t touched in two years doesn’t count), which one is bringing you the best people, and then build just one more.

EP 262 · 32 MIN LISTEN · 6 MIN READ

If Instagram disappeared tomorrow, would your business still know how to find new people?

That question has been rattling around in my brain this week after a conversation with a business owner who has around 150,000 Instagram followers and an email list of approximately 12,000 people.

Yep. You read that correctly.

She’s done incredibly fucking well on Instagram, and she still came to me asking, “How do I keep growing my email list if Instagram isn’t working the way it used to… and I don’t want to pay for ads?”

That got my attention, because if someone with 150K followers is asking what else is out there, we probably need to have a bigger conversation about where our growth actually comes from. So today, I’m giving you the options – no dancing for the algorithm, no throwing money at Meta, and no creating seven new platforms before breakfast.

Just a simple growth system you can actually stick with.

LINKS MENTIONED

→ Digital Shop: https://shop.kyliekelly.com

→ Free Resource: Your Next 1000 Subscribers Instant Access Here

→ My Free Community: Email Marketing Skool

WHAT YOU’LL LEARN IN THIS EPISODE

✅ Why visibility and social media are not the same thing

✅ The two growth lanes I’d choose: borrowed audiences + evergreen discovery

✅ How podcast guesting, summits, bundles and freebie swaps can grow your list

✅ Why SEO, Pinterest, PR and podcasting can become compounding business assets

✅ How your lead magnet turns visibility into actual email subscribers

✅ The three questions to ask before choosing your 90-day growth strategy

Instagram is one front door… not the whole fucking house

Somewhere along the way, online business taught us that “visibility” means social media.

Need more leads? Post more.
Need more sales? Post more.
Need more visibility? Reels, stories, carousels, TikTok, Threads, LinkedIn… and no bloody wonder everyone’s exhausted.

The truth is, social media is one visibility strategy. One.
Podcasting is another door. Google is another. Pinterest, PR, summits, bundles, podcast interviews, collaborations, referrals and guest teaching can all become different ways for the right people to discover you.

That’s why the question I want you asking isn’t, “How do I get better at Instagram?” It’s, “How do I create more opportunities for the right people to discover me?”

Or, as I said in the episode, how do we create a house full of fucking front doors?

Because when you think about visibility that way, Instagram stops being the entire business and becomes exactly what it should be – one option.

If Instagram vanished tomorrow, here’s what I’d do…

If Instagram disappeared tomorrow and I needed to grow my email list, I genuinely wouldn’t panic. I also wouldn’t immediately create accounts on seven different platforms and attempt to become a YouTuber-blogger-podcaster-Pinterest-girlie overnight, because that is a fast track to burning yourself out and deciding none of it works.

Instead, I would choose two growth lanes: one borrowed audience strategy and one evergreen discovery strategy.

One gives me the potential for quicker bursts of new people, while the other gives me something that can compound quietly in the background over time.

Then I’d connect both of those lanes to one really strong reason for somebody to join my email list. That’s the whole system. Not 12 strategies, not endless content, not trying to be everywhere – two lanes, one destination.

Lane One: Borrowed Audiences

If I wanted to grow more quickly without spending money on ads, borrowed audiences are where I’d begin. The beauty of this strategy is that you get to shortcut one of the hardest parts of marketing: distribution. Somebody else has already built the podcast, newsletter, community or audience, which means you don’t have to start from zero every single time.

Instead of asking, “How do I go and find 500 new people?” you get to ask, “Who already has a relationship with 500 of the kinds of people I would love to meet?” That is such a different way of approaching growth, and it’s one I’ve used over and over again in my own business.

Borrowed audience strategies can include podcast guesting, summits, bundles, freebie swaps, newsletter swaps, guest teaching and collaborations. You’re not turning up and saying, “Give me your audience.” You’re asking, “You serve these people, I serve these people… is there something genuinely useful we could create together?”

That matters because when collaborations are done well, the audience growth becomes a byproduct of the relationship. And those relationships? They can keep paying off for years.

Start simple: podcast guesting

Podcast guesting is one of my favourite borrowed audience strategies because you don’t need thousands of followers to make it work.

You need something useful to say, a clear angle, and a reason for somebody else’s audience to want to hear the conversation.

And please, don’t pitch a podcast host with, “Hi, I’m Kylie and I’m an email marketing strategist and I’d love to talk about email marketing.” Cool. So would 400 fucking other people.

Pitch the conversation instead.

What are you seeing in your industry? What do you have an opinion on? What story could you share? What useful transformation could you help their listener create?

Then, when you get on that podcast, don’t send everybody to your Instagram profile. This is your opportunity to move borrowed attention onto something you actually own. Give them a next step that makes sense based on the conversation you’ve just had, ideally a lead magnet that solves the exact problem you were talking about.

If I’ve just spent 30 minutes talking about how to grow without social media, sending people to kyliekelly.com/free to grab my Your Next 1,000 Subscribers guide makes sense.

It’s a natural continuation of the conversation, and that is what makes the whole thing work so beautifully.

Freebie swaps don’t need to generate 1,000 subscribers to work

This is where our brains love to sabotage a perfectly good strategy. You do a freebie swap, 30 people join your list, and immediately your brain goes, “That wasn’t enough.”

Excuse me?!

What if those were 30 perfect-fit potential clients?

If you did two swaps a month, that’s 60 new subscribers. Keep that going for a year and suddenly you’ve added 720 people to your email list through aligned recommendations – not random people, but people who already have a reason to be interested in what you do.

We need to stop looking for the lottery-ticket strategy and start respecting what consistency can compound into.

A small number of the right people, repeatedly, can build something incredibly valuable over time.

Lane Two: Evergreen Discovery

Borrowed audiences can give you faster bursts of growth, but I also want something in your business that keeps working when you’re not. I want you playing Monopoly with your kids, lying on a beach in the Maldives, sleeping, drinking coffee… whatever the fuck you’re doing – and something you created months ago can still introduce somebody new to your work.

That’s evergreen discovery.

It could look like SEO, blogging, Pinterest, YouTube, PR, your own podcast or strategically created search-led content.

The specific platform matters less than the principle: can I create something today that might still bring someone into my world six months from now?

That is what we’re aiming for, because I don’t want all of your growth to depend on you constantly being online, promoting, posting and creating from scratch.

Stop creating content. Start creating assets.

I’m becoming increasingly obsessed with this distinction. If I spend three hours creating something, I want that thing to work its fucking ass off.

Can Google find it? Can someone share it? Can Pinterest surface it? Can I reference it in an email? Can I send it to somebody next year? Can it rank for a useful search term? Can it bring a subscriber into my business while I’m nowhere near my laptop?

That’s an asset.

And assets compound. A blog post might do absolutely nothing tomorrow, which is the annoying part of evergreen strategies.

They are not always sexy at the beginning. But six months from now, someone could search the exact question you answered, find your article, download your freebie and join your email list. You weren’t even there. You created the thing once, and it kept working.

That is the kind of marketing machine I want you building.

Your lead magnet is the bridge

There is one very important piece missing from both growth lanes, and that’s your lead magnet. Because visibility on its own does not create an email list.

Imagine your visibility strategy brings people to one side of a bridge. On the other side is your email list — the place where the relationship continues, where people actually get to know you, where you can nurture them and eventually invite them into your offers.

Your lead magnet is the bridge between the two.

You could be featured on 20 podcasts, rank number one on Google, get 100,000 Pinterest views or appear in Forbes, but if there is no useful, relevant next step for someone to take, you’re basically renting attention and handing it straight back.

Your lead magnet doesn’t need to be some ridiculous 45-page ebook nobody is going to read. It needs to solve one clear problem for the exact person you want more of.

That person discovers you, thinks, “Oh my God, she understands my problem,” and then sees an obvious next step. They cross the bridge, join your list, and now email gets to do its job.

You can help them. Tell stories. Introduce your ideas. Invite them into things. Sell when it makes sense. Over time, they go from, “Who the fuck is Kylie?” to, “Oh my God, I love Kylie,” to, “Kylie has exactly what I need.”

That’s the journey.

Your simple 90-day growth plan

I want you to make this ridiculously simple. Grab a piece of paper and create two columns:

Borrowed Audiences and Evergreen Discovery.

Under each one, choose one strategy.

Then ask yourself three questions. Where does my ideal person already spend time? What kind of visibility am I actually good at? And can I realistically repeat this for 90 days?

That last question is especially important, because consistency is where the compounding happens. If you hate the thing you’ve chosen, you’re probably not going to keep doing it long enough to know whether it actually works.

And for the love of Ted Lasso, please don’t pick seven things.

I don’t want you coming back in three weeks saying, “Kylie, none of this worked,” only for me to ask how many podcast pitches you sent and hear “two,” or how many blog posts you wrote and hear “one,” or how long you tried Pinterest and hear “nine days.”

That is not enough data, my love.

Pick your two. Give them the full 90 days. Track what happens. Look at where subscribers are actually coming from, which opportunities are converting and which ones are bringing the right people into your world.

Then do more of what actually works.

title: Stop Creating New Offers [Here’s What I Would Do Instead]
